purpose: Nalbuphine is a strong pain reliever used to treat moderate to severe pain, such as pain after surgery or during labor. It can also be used to help with pain during certain medical procedures or as part of anesthesia care. Your doctor or nurse will give it to you when over-the-counter pain medicines are not enough.
how_it_works: Nalbuphine works by attaching to special receptors in your brain and body called opioid receptors, which help block pain signals. It acts like a pain reliever at some receptors while partially blocking others, which is why it is called a mixed opioid. This unique action means it can relieve pain effectively while having a lower risk of some serious opioid side effects like severe breathing problems.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include feeling sleepy or drowsy, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, sweating, a dry mouth, and headache. Some people may feel a sense of being disconnected or have unusual feelings. These effects are usually temporary and more common right after the injection.
warnings: Nalbuphine can slow your breathing, especially if you take other medicines that cause drowsiness, such as sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medicines, or alcohol. Do not drive or operate machinery while taking it. If you have been using other opioid pain medicines regularly, tell your doctor, because nalbuphine can trigger sudden withdrawal symptoms. It should be used very cautiously during pregnancy and is given only by a healthcare professional in a medical setting.
typical_dosing: Nalbuphine is given by injection into a vein, muscle, or under the skin — it is not a pill you take at home. A typical adult dose is 10 mg every 3 to 6 hours as needed for pain, but your doctor or nurse will adjust the dose based on your pain level and how your body responds. It is always given by a trained healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital setting.
